html:
This dua — Bismika Allāhumma amūtu wa aḥyā ("In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live") — is the shortest and most frequently recited of the Prophet's ﷺ sleep supplications. It is narrated by Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān and recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6324 (Kitāb al-Daʿawāt — the Book of Supplications), with the companion wake-up formula narrated in the same chain: Al-ḥamdu lillāhi alladhī aḥyānā baʿda mā amātanā wa ilayhi al-nushūr ("Praise be to Allah who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection").

What sets this dua apart is not its length but its claim. In seven Arabic words the sleeping Muslim submits the two hinges of existence — life and death — to the one who grants and withdraws them. Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī notes in Fatḥ al-Bārī that the Prophet ﷺ chose the identical phrasing for both sleep and death because al-manām akhū al-mawt — "sleep is the brother of death." The transition into unconsciousness each night is a rehearsal of the final transition. The formula teaches the believer to meet both the same way: in His name.

The sleep-death parallel in the Qur'an

The dua's theological ground is laid explicitly in two Qur'anic passages that classical mufassirs read as its direct source. Al-Zumar 39:42: "Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that die not during their sleep. He keeps those for which He has ordained death and sends the others back until an appointed term." Al-Anʿām 6:60: "It is He who takes your souls by night and knows what you have gained by day; then He raises you up again in it, that an appointed term may be fulfilled."

Ibn Kathīr, commenting on both verses, draws the structural reading the dua ratifies: every night the soul undergoes a minor wafāh (a lesser death-taking), and every morning a minor baʿth (a lesser resurrection). The believer who recites Bismika Allāhumma amūtu wa aḥyā enters this nightly rehearsal consciously. The wake-up formula — "Praise be to Allah who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection" — makes the parallel liturgical. Morning is the proof-of-concept the dua was asking for: if He returned my soul this morning, He will return it on the morning that has no night after it.

The nightly practice — fuller frame from Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 247

The brief Bismika formula sits inside a richer nightly sunna preserved by al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 247 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2710. Ibn Ḥajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī reconstructs the full sequence the Prophet ﷺ taught Al-Barāʾ: perform wudūʾ as for prayer; lie on the right side; place the right hand under the right cheek; then recite the longer formula that opens "Allāhumma aslamtu wajhī ilayka wa fawwaḍtu amrī ilayka" ("O Allah, I surrender my face to You and entrust my affair to You…") and closes with the Āmantu bi-kitābika alladhī anzalta wa bi-nabiyyika alladhī arsalta declaration of faith. The Prophet ﷺ then told Al-Barāʾ: "If you die in this night, you will die upon the fiṭra."

Ibn al-Qayyim al-Jawziyyah in Zād al-Maʿād treats this as the complete prophetic sleep protocol — the brief Bismika formula being the minimum acceptable discharge of the sunna, and the fuller Al-Barāʾ formula being the recommended practice when time and strength permit. Both are therapeutic in the sense Ibn al-Qayyim develops in al-Ṭibb al-Nabawī: the believer who closes the day with his tongue affirming surrender to Allah closes it with the soul in a state the fiṭra was designed for. If death comes in the night — and the dua explicitly contemplates this possibility — the soul meets it already oriented.

The cupping-blowing sunna of the three Quls

The second component of the Prophet's ﷺ nightly practice is the three-surah refuge formula narrated by ʿĀʾisha in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5017 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2192: "Whenever the Prophet ﷺ went to his bed every night, he would join his palms, blow into them, and recite over them Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ, Sūrat al-Falaq, and Sūrat al-Nās. Then he would wipe over as much of his body as he could reach, starting with his head and face and the front of his body. He would do this three times."

Al-Qurṭubī in al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qur'an and Ibn Ḥajar both treat this as a demonstrated ruqyah — a protective recitation sanctioned by the Prophet's ﷺ own personal practice. The three surahs are the ones Qurandaily covered in Q10 (al-Nās), Q11 (al-Falaq), and Q12 (al-Ikhlāṣ): sincerity of worship (al-Ikhlāṣ), refuge from external harm (al-Falaq), and refuge from the whisperer within (al-Nās). Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the Prophet ﷺ chose these three because they map the three domains from which night-time harm proceeds: the heart's wandering from pure monotheism, the external world's physical dangers (envy, darkness, witchcraft, destructive natural phenomena), and the internal world's intrusive thoughts and whispers.

Āyat al-Kursī — the protection narration

A third narration completes the classical sleep-protection corpus. Abū Hurayrah narrates in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2311 (and in muʿallaq form at 5010 — Ibn Ḥajar grades the chain ṣaḥīḥ) that a thief who attempted to steal from the zakāt stores Abū Hurayrah was guarding promised to teach him a verse that, if recited upon going to bed, would guarantee Allah's protection and that no shayṭān would approach him until morning. The verse was Āyat al-Kursī (Al-Baqarah 2:255). When Abū Hurayrah reported the incident to the Prophet ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ confirmed: "He told you the truth, though he is a liar. That was a shayṭān."

Ibn Ḥajar surfaces the moral: the testimony is true even when the witness is corrupt. The protective efficacy of Āyat al-Kursī does not depend on the moral standing of the one who first reported it, but on the One who sent down the verse. This fits the Bismika frame: the entire sleep formula is a redirection of trust away from any created agency — including one's own mental vigilance — toward Allah alone.

Reciting what the Prophet ﷺ recited vs reciting more than he did

A common pastoral question Qurandaily receives: should I combine every narrated bedtime formula into a single long ritual? Al-Nawawī's treatment in al-Adhkār is characteristically balanced. The minimum sunna is the brief Bismika Allāhumma amūtu wa aḥyā, which the Prophet ﷺ himself recited habitually. The recommended practice adds the three Quls with the cupping-blowing wipe, Āyat al-Kursī, and (where strength permits) the fuller Al-Barāʾ formula with its "I surrender my face to You" opening. The maximalist practice that adds the last two verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah (per the ḥadīth of Abū Masʿūd in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5040 — "whoever recites the last two verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah in a night, they will suffice him") is also well-attested.

What al-Nawawī discourages is the opposite error: inventing additional recitations not narrated from the Prophet ﷺ and treating them as pious supplements. The sunna is self-limiting. The believer who recites what the Messenger ﷺ recited has discharged the practice completely. Addition beyond the attested narrations risks introducing bidʿa — innovation — into the single act most intimately tied to the believer's final transit.

Why the Prophet ﷺ included death-language in a sleep formula

Modern readers sometimes find the Bismika Allāhumma amūtu wa aḥyā formula jarring. It is not comforting language. The dua does not say "O Allah, let me sleep well and wake refreshed." It says, flatly, "In Your name I die and I live." Ibn Taymiyyah in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā argues that this is precisely the formula's spiritual function: it refuses the Western-modern distinction between sleep (a safe, controllable transition) and death (a terrifying one). The believer who treats sleep as a nightly rehearsal for the final transit does not fear death as a stranger — he has been meeting it, under its lesser name, every evening of his life.

Ibn al-Qayyim develops the therapeutic consequence in al-Ṭibb al-Nabawī: anxiety about death diminishes in exact proportion to the practice of the sleep-dua. The person who nightly submits his soul in His name reaches the actual death moment having already said the formula ten thousand times. The journey is familiar. The One whose name opens the formula is familiar. What remains strange is only the finality — and that finality is the one feature the formula explicitly contemplates when it couples amūtu (I die) with wa aḥyā (and I live): both are "in Your name," and the one who speaks the name has already surrendered the outcome.

The companion wake-up formula and the resurrection parallel

The sleep dua is incomplete without its morning counterpart, narrated in the same Bukhārī 6324 chain: Al-ḥamdu lillāhi alladhī aḥyānā baʿda mā amātanā wa ilayhi al-nushūr ("Praise be to Allah who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection"). Three features Ibn Ḥajar highlights: (1) the past-tense amātanā ("He caused us to die") — ratifying the Qur'anic reading that sleep IS a form of death-taking; (2) the explicit coupling with al-nushūr (the final resurrection) — turning each morning into theological evidence; (3) the opening al-ḥamdu lillāh rather than a petition — because the thing being asked for in the sleep dua has already been granted, and the only remaining response is praise.

This pair — sleep-formula asking and morning-formula praising — is the complete liturgical frame. Reciting only the first (the common modern practice) does not break the sunna, but it leaves half the theology unspoken. The believer who completes both halves lives inside a 24-hour cycle in which every sleep is a surrender in His name and every waking is a resurrection in His praise.

What this dua is NOT

Carrying forward the honesty policy established in the Q14 anxiety-and-grief commentary: this sleep formula is NOT a sedative. It is NOT a cure for clinical insomnia (the Prophet ﷺ himself experienced sleepless nights, as narrated by ʿĀʾisha in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7439 regarding his restlessness before the Battle of Badr). It is NOT a guarantee against bad dreams or night-time disturbance in every individual case — Ibn Ḥajar notes that the sunna of changing sides and seeking refuge from a bad dream exists precisely because such disturbances still occurred to the Companions despite nightly recitation.

What the formula IS: the Prophet's ﷺ demonstrated practice for closing the day in a state of consciously-affirmed submission. Its efficacy is spiritual before it is psychological. The believer who recites it is not purchasing a quiet night; he is confessing that his night, quiet or disturbed, belongs to the One in whose name he dies and lives. This confession is what the sunna is actually asking him to perform. Everything downstream of that — restfulness, dream quality, waking energy — is a secondary consequence that may or may not follow, and whose absence does not falsify the primary spiritual act.
